biology_degree.caption: The degree runs from atoms to ecosystems; each box is a field you can open from the map.

bio_foundations.caption: Foundations are the habits and big ideas of the whole science, from the scientific method to its history.

bio_scientific_method.caption: Science is a loop: a hypothesis makes a prediction, the experiment tests it, and the result sends you back to refine the idea.

bio_themes_of_life.caption: Six ideas keep coming back in every chapter of biology; try to spot which one each new topic illustrates.

bio_levels_organization.caption: Each level of organisation is bigger than the last; on a log scale it spans about 17 orders of magnitude.

bio_characteristics_life.caption: Living things tick all of these boxes; a virus or a crystal fails at least one, which is why they are borderline cases.

shapes.text: one cell  →  two cells (never from non-living matter)

bio_cell_theory.caption: Watch the cell divide: every new cell comes from a pre-existing cell, never from nothing.

bio_homeostasis_concept.caption: With negative feedback (higher gain) the same disturbance causes a much smaller, but never zero, shift from the set point. Slide the gain.

bio_model_organisms.caption: Model organisms span 3 orders of magnitude in genome size, but all share core biology such as DNA, ribosomes and cell cycles.

bio_taxonomy_intro.caption: Taxonomy nests groups inside groups: three domains, then kingdoms below the eukaryotes. Every species sits at a leaf.

bio_experimental_basics.caption: The uncertainty of a mean shrinks as 1/sqrt(n): more replicates help, but with diminishing returns. Move the slider to change the variability.

bio_history_of_biology.caption: Slide the year forward to reveal milestones; discoveries came faster and faster once the molecular tools arrived.

bio_chem_life.caption: Life runs on a short list of chemical rules: bonds, water, pH, and energy.

bio_atoms_isotopes.caption: Isotopes of one element differ only in neutrons. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable; carbon-14 is radioactive (half-life 5,730 years).

shapes.text: valence electrons (outer shell): {Z<=2 ? Z : (Z<=10 ? Z-2 : Z-10)}

bio_electron_shells.caption: Electrons fill shells of 2, 8, 8. Raise the atomic number Z and watch the outer shell: carbon (6) has 4 valence electrons, neon (10) a full shell.

bio_ionic_covalent.caption: The bigger the electronegativity difference, the more a bond shifts from shared (covalent) to transferred (ionic). Slide Δχ to read the ionic character.

bio_polarity_hbonds.caption: Water is polar (O is δ−, H is δ+), so neighbours attract. A hydrogen bond (dashed) is ~20 kJ/mol, about 5% of an O–H bond. Pull the molecules apart past ~2.6 Å to break it.

bio_noncovalent_forces.caption: Two atoms attract at long range (van der Waals) and repel when they overlap. The minimum is the stable contact distance; deeper wells mean stickier surfaces.

bio_water_properties.caption: Liquid water is densest at about 4 °C, so ice floats and lakes freeze from the top down. Slide the temperature along the curve.

bio_solutions_concentration.caption: Osmotic pressure Π = i·c·R·T grows with the number of dissolved particles. At the same molarity NaCl (i = 2) pulls twice as hard as glucose.

bio_acids_bases_ph.caption: pH is −log₁₀[H⁺]: each unit is a tenfold change. Slide the pH and watch [H⁺] fall as [OH⁻] rises; they cross at pH 7 where both equal 10⁻⁷ M.

bio_buffers.caption: Around pH = pKa the curve is flat: a buffer works best within ±1 pH unit of its pKa. Change pKa to retune the buffer.
bio_buffers.xlabel: fraction of acid converted to base [A⁻]/total

bio_mole_molarity.caption: Diluting does not change the amount of solute: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂. Raise the final volume and the concentration drops as 1/V.

bio_reaction_equilibrium.caption: A ⇌ B settles where forward and reverse rates match, at [B]/[A] = K = kf/kr. Change the rate constants and watch the plateau move.

bio_reaction_kinetics.caption: Rate constants follow the Arrhenius law k ∝ exp(−Ea/RT). A bigger activation energy makes the reaction far more temperature-sensitive.

bio_thermo_laws.caption: Energy is conserved but spreads out: sunlight becomes chemical energy, work, and finally heat that raises the entropy of the surroundings.

bio_gibbs_free_energy.caption: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A process that absorbs heat (ΔH > 0) can still go if it increases disorder enough: the line crosses zero at T = ΔH/ΔS.

bio_redox_biology.caption: ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′: a bigger voltage drop between donor and acceptor releases more free energy per electron pair. Points show NADH and FADH₂ burning with O₂.

bio_atp_energy_coupling.caption: ATP hydrolysis is more favourable in cells than in the test tube because ATP is kept far above equilibrium relative to ADP. Slide [Pi] or read the curve at ATP/ADP ≈ 10.

bio_electrolytes_ions.caption: The Nernst equation gives the voltage at which an ion is at equilibrium across a membrane: E = (61.5/z)·log([out]/[in]) at 37 °C. Vary the outside K⁺.

bio_carbon_chemistry.caption: Carbon forms four strong, stable bonds (to C, H, O, N), and multiple bonds get stronger but shorter. That strength makes long chains and rings possible.

bio_macromolecule_synthesis.caption: Condensation joins monomers by removing water; hydrolysis splits polymers by adding it. Cells use the same bond with opposite enzymes.

bio_orgchem.caption: Organic chemistry gives the vocabulary (groups, shapes) and the verbs (reaction types) that biochemistry uses.

bio_functional_groups.caption: Seven groups account for most of the chemistry of life; the group, not the carbon skeleton, decides how a molecule behaves.

bio_isomers.caption: Isomers share a formula but differ in connectivity (structural) or in 3D arrangement (stereo). Glucose and fructose are structural isomers.

bio_chirality.caption: Looking down from the fourth group, the left molecule goes pink→blue→green clockwise; its mirror image goes the other way. Rotate the left one: no angle matches the right.

bio_fischer_cyclic_sugars.caption: In water, glucose sits mostly in two ring forms that interconvert through the open chain (mutarotation); the reactive aldehyde form is vanishingly rare.

bio_conformations.caption: Rotating about a C–C bond changes the energy: staggered forms (anti, gauche) are low, eclipsed ones are high. Raise the barrier to see a stiffer bond.

bio_acid_base_organic.caption: A group is half-protonated at pH = pKa. Carboxylates (pKa ≈ 4.8) are charged at body pH, while amines (pKa ≈ 10.6) stay protonated.

bio_nucleophile_electrophile.caption: A nucleophile (electron-rich, Nu⁻) donates a pair to an electrophile (δ+ carbon); the curved arrow tracks the electrons, and the leaving group departs.

bio_substitution_elimination.caption: SN2 rate rises with nucleophile concentration, SN1 does not (its slow step is the leaving group alone). Slide the substrate concentration.

bio_carbonyl_chemistry.caption: A nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; the intermediate either picks up a proton (addition, e.g. hemiacetal) or loses water (condensation, e.g. imine or aldol).

bio_acyl_substitution.caption: The tetrahedral intermediate collapses by expelling the best leaving group, so reactive acyl groups (thioesters, anhydrides) can safely hand the acyl to a better-bound partner.

bio_phosphoryl_transfer.caption: A kinase moves the terminal phosphate of ATP onto a target; a phosphatase takes it off. This on/off switch regulates much of the cell.

bio_redox_organic.caption: Each step up the ladder removes two hydrogens (or adds oxygen): the carbon oxidation state rises from −4 in methane to +4 in CO₂, releasing energy at each step.

bio_resonance_aromatic.caption: Resonance spreads electrons, so the peptide C–N and benzene C–C bonds are intermediate between single and double. That makes the peptide bond short, flat and rigid.

bio_spectroscopy_structure.caption: In ¹H NMR the CH₃ triplet and CH₂ quartet of ethanol reveal neighbouring hydrogens (n + 1 rule). Higher field strength narrows each multiplet in ppm.

bio_biochem.caption: The molecules (sugars, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids), the catalysts that act on them, and the pathways that link them.

shapes.text: anomer at C1: OH down = α, OH up = β

bio_monosaccharides.caption: Glucose closes into a six-membered ring; the new OH on C1 can point down (α) or up (β). Flip the slider to switch anomers.

bio_disaccharides.caption: Each disaccharide is two sugars joined by a glycosidic bond with loss of water: maltose (α1→4), lactose (β1→4), sucrose (α1→β2).

bio_polysaccharides.caption: Same monomer, different bond: α-1,4 chains coil into energy stores, while β-1,4 chains lie straight and H-bond into tough fibres.

bio_glycoconjugates.caption: Sugar chains on proteins and lipids form the glycocalyx, the cell's outer coat; the ABO blood groups are simply different glycolipid sugars.

bio_fatty_acids_fats.caption: Fat packs about twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate or protein because its carbons are more reduced and carry almost no water.

bio_membrane_lipids.caption: Phospholipids have a polar head (circle) and two nonpolar tails (lines); in water they self-assemble into a bilayer with tails hidden inside. Watch the heads jiggle.

bio_steroids_terpenoids.caption: All of these are built from five-carbon isoprene units; cholesterol is made via mevalonate, and statins block the step that commits carbon to it.

bio_amino_acids.caption: Amino acids carry charge that depends on pH. Net charge is zero at the pI (≈ 6.0 for glycine); acidic residues push it down, lysine pushes it up.

bio_peptide_bond.caption: The peptide bond (gold) has partial double-bond character, so six atoms stay in one plane. Slide n to see how length grows the sequence space (20ⁿ chains).

bio_protein_structure.caption: Secondary structure comes from backbone hydrogen bonds: helix (i to i+4, left) and β-strands side by side (dashed, right). Primary is the sequence; tertiary and quaternary fold and assemble these.

bio_protein_folding.caption: In urea a protein unfolds sharply, like a two-state switch. A more stable protein (bigger ΔG) needs more denaturant to reach the 50% midpoint.

bio_chaperones_proteostasis.caption: Chaperones give nascent chains a second chance to fold; proteins that still fail are tagged for destruction, otherwise they aggregate.

bio_ubiquitin_proteasome.caption: E1, E2 and E3 enzymes attach a chain of ubiquitin to a target; the 26S proteasome recognises the chain, unfolds the protein and chops it into peptides.

bio_hemoglobin_cooperativity.caption: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively (Hill n ≈ 2.8), giving an S-shaped curve: it loads in the lungs and unloads in tissues. Raise P50 to mimic the Bohr effect.

bio_protein_analysis.caption: Each purification step removes other proteins, raising the specific activity (activity per mg protein) by orders of magnitude.

bio_nucleotides.caption: A nucleotide is base + sugar + phosphate; the phosphodiester bond joins the 3′ OH of one sugar to the 5′ phosphate of the next, giving the chain direction.

bio_rna_types.caption: Most RNA in a cell is ribosomal RNA; the messenger RNAs that code for proteins are only a few percent of the total.

bio_enzyme_catalysis.caption: An enzyme does not change the reactant or product energies; it lowers the activation barrier by stabilising the transition state. Slide ΔΔG‡ to see the rate gain.
bio_enzyme_catalysis.xlabel: reaction coordinate  (S → ES → TS → EP → P)

shapes.text: ES complex: pocket closed around S

bio_active_site_induced_fit.caption: The substrate does not just fit a rigid lock: binding makes the enzyme close around it (induced fit). Slide to bring the substrate in.

bio_cofactors_coenzymes.caption: Many coenzymes are made from vitamins, so a vitamin deficiency stops the enzymes that need them. Each coenzyme shuttles one kind of chemical group.

bio_michaelis_menten.caption: Rate rises with substrate and levels off at Vmax; Km is the substrate level giving half of Vmax. Move both sliders and see which feature shifts.

bio_lineweaver_burk.caption: Plotting 1/v against 1/[S] straightens the Michaelis–Menten curve: the y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km. Change them and watch the intercepts move.

bio_enzyme_inhibition.caption: Competitive inhibitors raise apparent Km (Vmax unchanged); non-competitive ones lower Vmax; uncompetitive ones lower both. Slide [I] and compare each curve to the control.

bio_allostery.caption: Allosteric enzymes give an S-shaped rate curve. An activator (ATP here) shifts it left, an inhibitor (CTP) shifts it right, so small changes in substrate act like a switch.

bio_enzyme_conditions.caption: Rate climbs with temperature until the protein starts to unfold, then crashes, so each enzyme has an optimum. Slide the melting temperature to compare a human and a heat-loving enzyme.

bio_covalent_regulation.caption: Two covalent switches: cutting an inactive zymogen once turns it on for good, while phosphorylation flips an enzyme on and off reversibly.

bio_metabolism_overview.caption: Catabolism breaks big molecules down to release ATP and building blocks; anabolism spends ATP and reducing power to build them back up.

bio_glycolysis.caption: Glycolysis spends 2 ATP early (priming) and earns 4 later, netting 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose. Change the number of glucose molecules.

bio_fermentation.caption: Without oxygen NADH must be recycled to NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue: animals make lactate, yeast make ethanol and CO₂. Only 2 ATP per glucose result.

bio_pyruvate_oxidation.caption: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle: one carbon leaves as CO₂ and the rest becomes acetyl-CoA, making NADH.

bio_krebs_cycle.caption: Each turn of the cycle oxidises one acetyl group to 2 CO₂, making 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP (ATP). Oxaloacetate is regenerated, so the cycle can repeat.

bio_electron_transport_chain.caption: NADH and FADH₂ hand electrons down a series of carriers to O₂; complexes I, III and IV use the energy to pump protons (4, 4 and 2 H⁺) across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

bio_chemiosmosis_atp_synthase.caption: Protons flow back through ATP synthase and spin its rotor, which squeezes out ATP (about 3 per full turn). A larger proton-motive force spins it faster.

bio_beta_oxidation.caption: Each round of four steps shortens the fatty acid by two carbons, releasing acetyl-CoA, FADH₂ and NADH. Longer chains give far more ATP than glucose.

bio_gluconeogenesis.caption: Gluconeogenesis reverses glycolysis but bypasses its three irreversible steps with different enzymes (pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, FBPase-1, G6Pase). It costs 6 ATP-equivalents per glucose.

bio_pentose_phosphate_pathway.caption: The oxidative branch turns glucose-6-phosphate into ribulose-5-P, making 2 NADPH and a CO₂; the rest either gives ribose for nucleotides or recycles into glycolysis.

bio_amino_acid_catabolism.caption: Amino groups are moved to α-ketoglutarate, then released as ammonium; the liver's urea cycle turns toxic NH₄⁺ into urea, using aspartate as a second nitrogen donor.

bio_fatty_acid_synthesis.caption: Fatty acid synthase adds two carbons per cycle, starting from malonyl-CoA and spending 2 NADPH each time; seven cycles make 16-carbon palmitate.

bio_photosynthesis_overview.caption: Light reactions in the thylakoid make ATP and NADPH and release O₂; the Calvin cycle in the stroma uses them to fix CO₂ into sugar.

bio_light_reactions.caption: Light lifts electrons to a high energy twice (the Z-scheme): photosystem II then I. Between the two the electron falls and its energy pumps protons; at the end it reduces NADP⁺ to NADPH.

bio_calvin_cycle.caption: Rubisco fixes CO₂ onto RuBP; ATP and NADPH reduce the product to G3P, and five-sixths of the G3P is recycled to RuBP. Three turns give one net G3P.

bio_metabolic_regulation.caption: PFK-1, the glycolysis gatekeeper, is inhibited by ATP: more ATP shifts its S-shaped curve to the right, so glycolysis slows when energy is plentiful.

bio_metabolic_integration.caption: In fasting, liver glycogen runs out within about a day while ketone bodies rise, so the brain can switch fuels. Slide the glycogen store to see how long it lasts.

bio_cell_biology.caption: A cell is a membrane-bound compartment with transport, organelles, a skeleton, signalling and a life cycle.

bio_prokaryote_eukaryote.caption: A bacterium (left, ~2 µm) has a nucleoid but no nucleus or organelles; a eukaryotic cell (right, 10–100 µm) has a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Not to scale.

bio_cell_size_limits.caption: As a cell grows its surface-to-volume ratio (3/r) falls while diffusion across it slows as r²/6D, so large cells need transport systems. Change the diffusion coefficient.

bio_fluid_mosaic.caption: The bilayer is a fluid with proteins floating in it, cholesterol tucked between lipids. Raise the temperature slider to make everything jiggle more (more fluid).

bio_diffusion_osmosis.caption: Diffusion spreads a concentration step: the front moves only as √(Dt), so doubling the distance takes four times as long. Slide time to watch the profile flatten.

bio_facilitated_transport.caption: Simple diffusion rises linearly with the gradient; a carrier saturates (like an enzyme) at Vmax because only so many proteins exist. Change the carrier's Km.

bio_active_transport.caption: Each pump cycle exports 3 Na⁺ and imports 2 K⁺ for one ATP, building the gradients (Na⁺ 145 vs 12 mM, K⁺ 5 vs 140 mM) that power signalling and transport.

bio_bulk_transport.caption: Endocytosis pinches the membrane inward to take in cargo; exocytosis fuses vesicles with the membrane to release it. Both are driven by coats, SNAREs and the cytoskeleton.

bio_membrane_potential.caption: The resting potential lies between E_K (≈ −90 mV) and E_Na (≈ +60 mV), weighted by relative permeability (GHK equation). Open Na⁺ channels (higher pNa/pK) and the membrane depolarises.

bio_nuclear_organization.caption: The nuclear envelope is perforated by pores; proteins with a nuclear-localisation signal enter and mRNA/ribosome subunits leave. The nucleolus builds ribosomes.

bio_protein_targeting_secretory.caption: Proteins with a signal peptide enter the ER while being made, then travel ER → Golgi → vesicles to the cell surface or lysosome; proteins without it stay in the cytosol.

bio_autophagy.caption: When starved, cells wrap parts of themselves in a double membrane (autophagosome) and deliver it to lysosomes, recycling the building blocks.

bio_endosymbiosis.caption: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from engulfed bacteria. Evidence: own circular DNA, 70S-like ribosomes, double membranes, and division by fission.

bio_chloroplasts_plastids.caption: Thylakoid membranes stack into grana inside a stroma; light reactions occur in the stacks and the Calvin cycle in the stroma. Other plastids store starch or pigments.

bio_cell_wall_ecm.caption: Each kingdom builds its outside layer from a different polymer; animal cells instead secrete a flexible extracellular matrix.

bio_cell_junctions.caption: Four main junctions between animal cells: seal the sheet, anchor to neighbours, link to the skeleton, or open channels for sharing small molecules.

bio_microtubules_motors.caption: Kinesin walks cargo toward the + end in 8 nm steps, and dynein walks the other way. Lower the ATP slider and the motors slow down (Michaelis–Menten).

bio_actin_intermediate.caption: The three filament systems differ in thickness and job: thin actin for shape and movement, mid-sized intermediate filaments for mechanical strength, thick microtubules for tracks.

bio_signaling_overview.caption: A signal is received, relayed through a chain of molecules and answered; each relay step amplifies. Change how many molecules each step activates.

bio_gpcr_signaling.caption: A ligand activates a GPCR, which swaps GDP for GTP on a G protein; the G protein turns on adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP, which activates PKA. GTP hydrolysis turns it off.

bio_rtk_cascades.caption: Growth factor binding dimerises the receptor, which phosphorylates itself; adaptor proteins switch on Ras, and a three-kinase cascade (Raf, MEK, ERK) carries the message to the nucleus.

bio_second_messengers.caption: Calcium signals are spikes: resting ≈ 100 nM jumps ~10-fold then is pumped back. A stronger stimulus makes the cell spike more often (frequency coding).

bio_nuclear_receptors.caption: Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble: they cross the membrane, bind a receptor that moves to the nucleus, and the receptor then switches genes on at hormone response elements.

bio_cell_cycle.caption: The cycle has four phases: G1 (grow), S (copy DNA), G2 (prepare), M (divide). Most of the difference between fast- and slow-dividing cells is in G1; slide it.

bio_cell_cycle_control.caption: Cyclins rise and fall in sequence, switching on CDKs that push the cycle forward. Raise DNA damage and p53 blocks the later cyclins, arresting the cell.

bio_cytokinesis_prokaryotic_division.caption: In binary fission the cell elongates, copies its DNA, and a ring of FtsZ constricts the middle until two identical cells separate; animal cells use an actin–myosin ring instead.

bio_apoptosis.caption: Intrinsic (mitochondrial) and extrinsic (death-receptor) pathways converge on executioner caspases, which dismantle the cell neatly so neighbours aren't harmed.

bio_stem_cells_differentiation.caption: Potency narrows as cells specialise: the zygote can make everything, embryonic stem cells any body cell, adult stem cells only their tissue's cell types.

bio_telomeres_senescence.caption: Telomeres shorten with each division until they hit a critical length and the cell stops (the Hayflick limit). Active telomerase slows the loss.

bio_molecular.caption: DNA is stored, copied, repaired, transcribed, translated, and regulated; each stage has its own machinery.

shapes.text: base pairs: A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds); pitch 3.4 nm, 10.5 bp/turn

bio_dna_structure.caption: Two antiparallel strands wind into a right-handed helix; the rungs are base pairs. Slide the length to convert base pairs into nanometres and mass.

bio_chromatin_packaging.caption: DNA is wound around histones into nucleosomes, then folded into fibres, loops and finally a mitotic chromosome, making it about 10,000 times shorter.

bio_central_dogma.caption: Information normally flows DNA → RNA → protein. Replication copies DNA; reverse transcription (some viruses) and RNA replication are the main exceptions.

bio_replication_machinery.caption: Helicase unzips the parental DNA; the leading strand grows continuously, the lagging strand in short Okazaki fragments. Slide the fork speed to see how long a genome takes.

bio_dna_damage_repair.caption: Different lesions need different repair crews; defects in these pathways cause cancer-prone syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum and Lynch syndrome.

bio_recombination_transposons.caption: Transposons hop: cut-and-paste elements move by a transposase, while retrotransposons copy via RNA and reverse transcriptase, which is why they fill much of our genome.

bio_genetic_code.caption: Read the code by first base (row), second base (column) and third base (U, C, A, G within each cell). * is a stop codon; AUG (M) starts translation. Single-letter amino acids.

shapes.text: transcription bubble ≈ 17 bp  ·  RNA 8–9 nt hybrid

bio_transcription_prokaryotic.caption: The polymerase (σ factor finds the promoter) melts a small bubble and slides along the template, reading 3′→5′ and growing the RNA 5′→3′. Slide the rate to speed it up.

bio_transcription_eukaryotic.caption: Eukaryotes need general transcription factors before Pol II can start: TFIID binds the TATA box, others recruit Pol II, and TFIIH unwinds DNA and phosphorylates the polymerase tail.

bio_rna_processing.caption: Pre-mRNA gets a 5′ cap and a poly(A) tail, and the spliceosome removes introns (grey) and joins the exons. Slide to carry out the splicing.

bio_trna_translation_machinery.caption: The ribosome reads mRNA three bases at a time: tRNAs bring amino acids to the A site, the P site holds the growing chain, and the ribosome then steps one codon along.

bio_translation_regulation_ptm.caption: Cells control how much protein is made (initiation factors, microRNAs) and then tune each protein with chemical tags (phosphate, sugar, ubiquitin) or cleavage.

bio_lac_operon.caption: The lac operon turns on only when lactose is present (repressor released) and glucose is low (cAMP–CAP activates). Raise glucose and the induced level drops.

bio_eukaryotic_gene_regulation.caption: Activators bound to distant enhancers loop DNA to the promoter via Mediator, recruiting Pol II; repressors and silencers do the opposite. Different TF combinations give each cell type its pattern.

bio_epigenetics.caption: Marks on DNA and histones switch chromatin between open and closed states without changing the sequence: acetylation opens, methylation of CpG islands closes.

bio_x_inactivation_imprinting.caption: In each female cell one X is randomly silenced by Xist RNA early in development, so women are mosaics (calico cats). Imprinted genes are silenced according to parent of origin.

bio_noncoding_rna.caption: Precursor miRNAs are trimmed by Drosha and Dicer; the mature strand guides the RISC complex (Argonaute) to matching mRNAs, which are degraded or blocked.

bio_post_transcriptional_control.caption: After transcription starts, mRNA level rises toward k·t½/ln2. Short-lived mRNAs respond fast and decline fast; stable ones respond slowly. Change the half-life.

bio_cancer_gene_regulation.caption: Proto-oncogenes are accelerators: one gain-of-function mutation makes them stuck on. Tumour suppressors (p53, Rb) are brakes: usually both copies must be lost.

bio_genetics.caption: Genetics starts with Mendel and crosses, adds chromosomes, mutation and pedigrees, then scales up to populations.

params.label: at least k with dominant trait

bio_mendel_laws.caption: Aa × Aa gives each offspring a 3/4 chance of the dominant phenotype. The bars show how many of n offspring show it; the shaded part is P(at least k).

bio_alleles_genotype.caption: Each gene sits at the same locus on two homologous chromosomes. Choose the allele combination: only aa shows the recessive phenotype.

bio_genetics_probability.caption: Independent events multiply, alternatives add. For a 1/4 risk per child, the chance that at least one of n children is affected is 1 − (3/4)ⁿ. Change the per-child risk.

bio_punnett_squares.caption: Each parent's gametes go along an edge; the squares show every offspring genotype. Choose the parental genotypes (0 = aa, 1 = Aa, 2 = AA) and read the ratio.

bio_dihybrid_assortment.caption: Crossing two double heterozygotes (AaBb × AaBb) gives four phenotypes in 9:3:3:1. Change the number of offspring to see the expected counts.

bio_dominance_extensions.caption: Phenotype versus the number of A alleles: with complete dominance the heterozygote matches AA; with incomplete dominance it sits halfway; slide h to move between them.
bio_dominance_extensions.xlabel: copies of allele A (0 = aa, 1 = Aa, 2 = AA)

bio_epistasis_pleiotropy.caption: In Labradors gene E (pigment deposition) is epistatic to gene B (black or brown): ee dogs are yellow whatever B they carry, giving a 9:3:4 ratio.

bio_meiosis_variation.caption: With n chromosome pairs, independent assortment alone gives 2ⁿ different gametes; humans (n = 23) make 8.4 million before crossing over adds far more.

bio_chromosome_theory.caption: Sutton and Boveri noticed that Mendel's hereditary factors behave exactly like chromosomes; Morgan's white-eyed flies tied one gene to the X chromosome.

bio_linkage_mapping.caption: Genes close together are rarely separated by crossing over, so recombination frequency is nearly equal to map distance; it saturates at 50% (unlinked). Slide the distance.

bio_sex_linkage.caption: X-linked recessive trait with a carrier mother: sons get one X, so half are affected. If the father is affected too, daughters can also be affected.

bio_pedigree_analysis.caption: Squares are males, circles females. Two unaffected carriers (Aa) have an affected child (aa): the trait skips a generation, typical of recessive inheritance. Press play to trace it.

bio_mutations.caption: Point mutations are classified by what they do to the protein: silent, missense (sickle-cell: Glu→Val), nonsense (early stop), or frameshift (indel not a multiple of 3).

bio_chromosomal_aberrations.caption: The risk of a child with trisomy 21 rises steeply with maternal age because eggs sit arrested in meiosis for decades. Slide the age to read the risk.

bio_single_gene_disorders.caption: The chance an offspring is affected depends on the mode of inheritance: recessive (both parents carriers) 25%, dominant 50%, X-linked recessive sons of a carrier 50%, mitochondrial from an affected mother nearly 100%.

bio_quantitative_traits.caption: Parents who are above average have offspring above average, but regressed toward the mean by (1 − h²). The slope of this line is the narrow-sense heritability h².

bio_gwas.caption: Each point is a variant; the height is −log₁₀ p. Real associations stand above the genome-wide significance line (p = 5×10⁻⁸); larger samples reveal weaker loci. Increase the sample size.

bio_population_genetics.caption: Allele frequencies come from genotype counts: each AA carries two A alleles, each Aa one. Enter the counts to calculate p and q.

bio_hardy_weinberg.caption: With random mating and no evolution, genotype frequencies settle at p², 2pq and q² after one generation. Heterozygotes peak at 50% when p = q = 0.5.

bio_drift_flow_selection_pop.caption: Natural selection with advantage s changes allele frequency along an S-curve: p(t) = p₀eˢᵗ / (1 − p₀ + p₀eˢᵗ). Slide s and p₀; with s = 0 nothing moves (drift aside).

bio_inbreeding_conservation_genetics.caption: In a small population inbreeding rises each generation (F = 1 − (1 − 1/2N)ᵗ) and fitness falls (exp(−B·F)). Smaller N means faster loss.

bio_genomics.caption: Biotechnology reads, copies, cuts and edits DNA, and bioinformatics makes sense of the data.

shapes.text: − at top (wells), + at bottom: small DNA runs furthest

bio_gel_electrophoresis.caption: DNA is negatively charged, so it moves toward + through the gel; smaller fragments move further, with distance roughly proportional to −log(size). Change the sample size and the gel percentage.

bio_pcr.caption: Each cycle can at most double the target: N = N₀(1+E)ⁿ. With 90% efficiency 30 cycles still gives ~10⁸-fold, but small efficiency losses compound. Slide cycles and efficiency.

bio_restriction_cloning.caption: The same restriction enzyme cuts vector and insert, leaving matching sticky ends; DNA ligase seals them, and antibiotic selection finds the bacteria that took up the plasmid.

bio_recombinant_expression.caption: Put the gene behind a strong inducible promoter in a vector, add the inducer (IPTG), then lyse the cells and capture the His-tagged protein on a nickel column.

bio_sanger_sequencing.caption: A small fraction r of nucleotides are chain-terminating ddNTPs, so each fragment length n appears with probability r(1−r)ⁿ⁻¹. Lower r gives longer reads but fewer short ones.

fns.label: share of fragments of length n (%)

bio_ngs.caption: Next-generation sequencers read millions of molecules in parallel: output per run is up to ten million times a Sanger capillary run.

bio_genome_assembly.caption: Reads land randomly, so the fraction of the genome covered is 1 − e^(−c) (Lander–Waterman). Coverage c = N·L/G; slide the read count to see when gaps disappear.

bio_transcriptomics.caption: RNA-seq turns the set of active transcripts into counts: isolate RNA, make cDNA, sequence, align reads to the genome, count per gene and test for differences between conditions.

bio_proteomics_omics.caption: Omics layers build on each other: the genome is the same in every cell, while transcripts, proteins and metabolites change; integrating them is systems biology.

bio_crispr_cas9.caption: A guide RNA leads Cas9 to a 20-nt match next to an NGG PAM; Cas9 cuts both strands, and repair either breaks the gene (NHEJ) or copies in a supplied edit (HDR).

bio_gmo_transgenics.caption: A gene of interest is delivered (Agrobacterium or gene gun) into plant cells, which are regenerated into whole plants; every cell then carries the transgene.

bio_gene_therapy.caption: A harmless virus (often AAV) delivers a working gene. In vivo it is injected into the body; ex vivo the patient's cells are corrected in the lab and returned.

bio_dna_fingerprinting_blotting.caption: Each STR locus gives a genotype shared by only a few percent of people; independent loci multiply. With 13 CODIS loci the random-match probability is about 10⁻¹⁵.

bio_sequence_alignment.caption: An alignment is scored: matches add, mismatches and gaps subtract. Change the scores and see how the total alignment score changes.

bio_blast_databases.caption: BLAST reports an E-value, the number of hits expected by chance: E ≈ m·n·2⁻ˢ. A bigger database or longer query needs a higher bit score to be significant.

bio_phylogenetic_methods.caption: Clustering by similarity builds a tree: the two closest sequences (human, chimp) join first, then others are added in order of distance. Press play to follow the order of joining.

bio_comparative_human_genomics.caption: The more recently two species shared an ancestor, the more alike their DNA: chimpanzees differ from us by only ~1–2% in aligned sequence.

bio_metagenomics.caption: The more DNA you sequence from a community, the more species you find, with diminishing returns (rarefaction). Rare species need very deep sequencing.

bio_microbiology.caption: Microbiology covers bacteria, archaea, viruses and microbial eukaryotes, plus infection, drugs and control.

bio_bacterial_structure.caption: A rod-shaped bacterium: a peptidoglycan wall around the membrane, a nucleoid without a nuclear envelope, ribosomes, pili for attachment and a flagellum whose wave drives swimming.

bio_microbial_growth.caption: Growth has four phases: lag, exponential (log) growth, stationary and death. A shorter generation time makes a steeper log phase; the lag depends on conditions.

bio_microbial_metabolism.caption: Microbes are classified by where they get energy (light or chemicals) and carbon (CO₂ or organic molecules); humans are chemoheterotrophs.

bio_horizontal_gene_transfer.caption: Bacteria swap genes sideways in three ways: through a pilus (conjugation), by taking up free DNA (transformation), or carried by phages (transduction).

bio_bacterial_diversity.caption: Bacteria include many phyla; a few big ones hold most cultured species: Proteobacteria (E. coli), Firmicutes (Bacillus), Actinobacteria (M. tuberculosis) and Cyanobacteria.

bio_archaea.caption: Archaea thrive where most life cannot. Growth rate peaks at an optimum and collapses just above it; a mesophile, a thermophile and a hyperthermophile have optima 70 °C apart. Slide a custom optimum.

bio_viruses_structure.caption: A virus is a genome (DNA or RNA) in a protein capsid, sometimes wrapped in a lipid envelope studded with spike proteins. Typical sizes are 20–300 nm; the envelope makes it fragile to soap.

bio_viral_life_cycles.caption: Every virus must attach to a host cell, get in, copy its genome and make capsid proteins using host machinery, assemble new particles, and leave by lysis or budding.

bio_bacteriophages.caption: In a one-step growth curve the phage titre stays flat during the eclipse and latent period, then jumps by the burst size when cells lyse. Slide both.

bio_retroviruses_hiv.caption: HIV binds CD4 and a co-receptor, its RNA is copied to DNA by reverse transcriptase, integrase inserts it into our genome as a provirus, and new virions bud out. Drugs target RT, integrase and protease.

bio_viroids_prions.caption: Viroids are bare circular RNAs; prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid; viruses carry a genome in a capsid. All three can be infectious.

bio_emerging_viruses.caption: Early in an outbreak cases grow exponentially at rate (R₀ − 1)/Tg. A higher R₀ gives a much faster rise and a higher herd-immunity threshold 1 − 1/R₀.

bio_protists.caption: Protists are not one group but several eukaryotic lineages: amoebae, alveolates (ciliates, Plasmodium), stramenopiles (diatoms, kelp) and excavates (Giardia, trypanosomes).

bio_human_microbiome.caption: Microbial density rises dramatically down the gut: the stomach is nearly sterile while the colon holds about 10¹¹ cells per gram.

bio_pathogenesis.caption: The chance of infection rises with dose, P = 1 − e^(−r·dose). The ID₅₀ (dose infecting half of hosts) is ln2 / r, so highly virulent pathogens have a tiny ID₅₀.

bio_antibiotics.caption: Above the MIC the kill rate beats the growth rate and the population falls; below it bacteria keep growing. Slide the dose as a multiple of the MIC.

bio_antibiotic_resistance.caption: Under drug pressure a tiny resistant minority takes over: p(t) follows the logistic curve with selection s. Higher selection or a larger starting fraction shortens the time.

bio_microbial_control.caption: Heat kills exponentially: log₁₀N falls by 1 every D minutes, and D shrinks tenfold for every z °C. Raise the temperature to sterilise faster.

bio_biofilms_quorum.caption: Cells release autoinducer, so its level tracks population density; a gene switches on abruptly past a threshold density (quorum sensing). Slide the threshold and sharpness.

bio_development.caption: Development runs from fertilisation through cleavage and gastrulation to organs, guided by gradients and gene switches.

bio_fertilization.caption: The sperm crosses the egg coat after an acrosome reaction; fusion triggers a calcium wave that hardens the coat and blocks other sperm, then the pronuclei merge.

bio_cleavage_blastula.caption: Cleavage divides the egg into more and more cells without growth, so each cell gets smaller as 1/2ⁿ. Slide the number of divisions.

bio_gastrulation_germ_layers.caption: Gastrulation produces three germ layers; every organ derives from one of them. Ectoderm makes skin and nerves, mesoderm muscle and blood, endoderm the gut lining and liver.

bio_neurulation_organogenesis.caption: The notochord induces the neural plate, whose edges fold up and fuse into the neural tube (future brain and spinal cord); neural crest cells migrate out and somites form beside it.

bio_morphogens_gradients.caption: A morphogen decays exponentially from its source, C = C₀e^(−x/λ). Cells read thresholds: high = one fate, medium = another, low = a third (the French-flag model). Change λ or the source strength.

bio_hox_developmental_genes.caption: Hox genes lie on the chromosome in the same order as the body regions they pattern (colinearity): front genes specify the head end, rear genes the tail end.

bio_developmental_signaling.caption: A handful of conserved pathways run the whole embryo, reused in different tissues to set axes, make boundaries and tell cells what to become.

bio_organoids_regeneration.caption: After amputation a salamander forms a blastema of dedifferentiated cells that re-grows the limb; metamorphosis is a hormone-triggered remodelling, e.g. tadpole to frog.

bio_human_prenatal_development.caption: Human development is dated from fertilisation; the embryonic period (weeks 3–8) builds all the organ systems, and later growth refines them.

bio_plant_embryogenesis_note.caption: The plant zygote divides asymmetrically to make an embryo (globular, heart, torpedo stages) with a root and shoot pole; the seed dries and stays dormant until water triggers germination.
